utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Planojevic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Planojevic.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As with all other witnesses speaking Serbian, I need to ask you to speak slowly so as to have everything in the transcript and to pause between my questions and your answers so that everything is properly recorded. Mr. Planojevic, did you provide a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have two corrections to make though, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have in e-court 1D7960.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see before you your statement?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you read it and signed it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could the last page be shown to the witness. Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You noticed that something was not reflected accurately and you said you wanted to make certain corrections.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: By your leave, I would go about it immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which paragraph and which piece of information does it refer to?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Item 2, page 1, the last two -- two words. Instead of "BiH government," it is actually the "council of ministers of BiH." That is the exact name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That has been taken note of. Tell us if there's any other substantive fact that needs to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Item 25, the last sentence where it reads that the Zelimir family had their car stolen. Actually, the person in question is Par Zelimir rather than a couple of people by the name of Zelimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you're saying that his first name is Par, last name Zelimir?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: First name Zelimir, last name Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you notice anything else?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I seem to have sped up. I asked you if there was anything else. It isn't your fault. It is entirely mine. In any case, you said that there were no other corrections to be made.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said that there were no other corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Taking into account the two corrections, otherwise does the statement accurately reflect what you said?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions today in the courtroom, would your answers be basically the same?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I could add certain clarifications to those answers previously provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope we will have that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this statement be admitted under 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there's no associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit his Rule 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3197, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to read out the summary of Mr. Dobrislav Planojevic's statement in the English language. [In English] Dobrislav Planojevic was born on 22nd of August, 1955, in Zakomo, Rogatica municipality. He was a professional police officer. He entered the service in 1973. Mr. Planojevic held various positions until he became chief of crime prevention and detection administration in February 1985, and chief of the SJB Novo Sarajevo in September 1987. From early June 1991 to April the 4th, 1992, he was the commander of the police station in Marin Dvor Centar municipality of Sarajevo. On 19th of April, 1992, he was appointed assistant minister for crime prevention and detection until the second half of July 1992. In September 1992, Mr. Planojevic joined the RS state security and worked as an inspector until 1st of July, 1994, when he became chief of State Security Service for the region of Sarajevo. Regarding the distribution of weapons to the reserve police, on 18th of September, 1991, Mr. Dobrislav Planojevic was informed that around 90 per cent of the weapons went to the Muslims, including not only the reserve policemen but also the new Muslim men who were enlisted. He checked the list of the supposed reserve policemen and found the names of 32 criminals, namely, men with prior convictions. Around 4th of April, 1992, shooting began in the city. The Green Berets attacked their police station and some of the Serbs' lives were in danger. For example, Pero Petrovic, a policeman of Serbian ethnicity, was killed at the Novo Sarajevo station, and another, Lazar Bojanic, was beaten up. Dobrislav Planojevic was aware that there was agreement to divide the MUP according to which the Serbian personnel were supposed to be accommodated at the high school of internal affairs in Vrace. When they crossed the bridge over the Miljacka on their way to Vrace, they noticed all the armed men, both policemen and civilians along the road. They were stopped but still passed. Eventually, they arrived at the local commune building in Vrace. In Vrace, the Muslims continuously fired at them from small-arms and artillery weapons. In early June 1992, the ministry was relocated to Kalovita Brda, Pale, and Kosuta hotel on Jahorina mountain. Regarding to the MUP, RS MUP, they had five CSBs: Sarajevo, Banja Luka, Doboj, Trebinje, and Bijeljina. However, they encountered numerous problems. One was that the shortage of professional staff. Another problem was that the deployment of its personnel on the front lines, and during which many policemen were killed. Furthermore, because of the ongoing combat investigating crimes were very difficult -- was very difficulty. For example, two corps of the BH army attacked the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps of the VRS around Sarajevo, a vast combat operation zone. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps were outnumbered by the BH army at the rate of five soldiers to one. At the outbreak of the conflict, there was widespread plunder. Criminal groups appeared everywhere. As for war crimes, Dobrislav Planojevic never received any written report about it. The only possible related incidence he knew was in Lukavica, where two Muslims were killed, after which he filed a criminal report and prosecuted the perpetrators. Dobrislav Planojevic insisted on fighting crime, by taking all appropriate steps, with maximum efforts on all occasions. Mr. Dobrislav Planojevic said he met with President Karadzic several times during the armed conflict. Each time the president insisted that the law had to be observed and gave them support for their work. And that is the summary, and I don't have additional questions for Mr. Planojevic at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Planojevic, as you may have noted, your evidence in-chief in this case has been admitted in writing; that is, through your written statement in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, but before doing so, I find it helpful if I give this advice to you: I'd like to draw your attention to a certain Rule that we have here at the international Tribunal; that is, Rule 90 (E) of Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Under this Rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges, if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that would amount to admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that provides evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and, as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would -- would ensure that such -- your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Planojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, before we begin, I would like to advise you of three matters. First, the Court asks us to be particularly concise during the cross-examination because we have very limited time. And to that end, I wish to focus on a number of issues, and I would ask you to respond to my questions on these topics in the most concise possible way.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Secondly, I note from your interview in 2004 that you had with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor and also in your testimony in 2010 in the Stanisic/Zupljanin trial that you tend to speak very quickly. And I would kindly ask you to try to speak at a slower pace so that everything you say is captured on the transcript so we don't constantly have to have interruptions to get you to repeat your answers.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And thirdly, as you know, everything we say has to be translated into a number of languages and therefore if you can -- if it's possible for you to follow the cursor on the screen in front of you, and when it comes -- when it stops after the letter A, then you can begin your answer. And when you finished your hopefully concise answer, if I'm not immediately asking you a question, it's not because I want you to continue elaborating on your answer, it's because I'm waiting for the interpretation to be completed.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Planojevic. The government's priority was to ensure war crimes against Serbs were documented and criminally investigated by the RS MUP, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: The priority was to document all crimes, at least at the place I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, I -- we can go through a few documents now, but -- but your superior, Mico Stanisic, the minister of the RS MUP, ordered his CSB chiefs to include in their daily report, information on their activities in the "collection of information and documents on war crimes against the Serbs." And which included "conducting an on-site investigation with the entire team in all cases of crimes against the Serbs." He issued that order on the 16th of May, 1992. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't recall that order.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P02715 [Realtime transcript read in error "P20715"].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give us the exhibit number again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where? In our case?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit number should have four digits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Not 2-0, "02715," yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, do you see here Mr. Stanisic is saying to collect documents on the crimes against the Serbian population?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the document now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit D00410, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: These are minutes of the government session held on the 24th of May, 1992, where the government asks the MUP to prepare as soon as possible for the use of the government: "Complete and exhaustive information on the security situation and the state of public order and peace in the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." And the following day -- and this is 65 ter number 18388.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If that could be brought up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I kindly ask to be told exactly where that task is cited? I see the Elektroprivreda company here and nothing on security. Is it perhaps on the next page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we see here down at the bottom of the page in English, it is under agenda item 2 and it says: "Special attention should be paid to issues of crime, protection of state and personal property of Serb people." I see the B/C/S document is a -- is a different document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It has been changed. Do you like to see it again, Mr. Karadzic, or is it okay to proceed?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to see it because the question was put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Can you go back to the previous document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is his page 2, which is ERN number 326.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably next page. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Planojevic, I appreciate that you weren't at this government session, therefore, I want to show you the next -- the document that was issued the next day which did go to the RS MUP, and that's 65 ter number 18388, where Branko Djeric requests the minister of internal affairs to "gather information and deliver a report to the government on the security of people and property in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." And, here, he says specifically in relation to -- specifically in relation to facts about vehicles from the TAS Sarajevo car factory compound in Vogosca and oil in Ilidza. Now this letter to the RS MUP doesn't make any specific request for information concerning violations of human rights or international humanity law. But acting on this request, Mr. Stanisic sent to five -- the five CSBs some instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And before we leave this document, if we could just go to the second page in the English. Yeah, we can see it is signed by Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: On the 26th of May, if we could go to 65 ter number 10834, Mr. Stanisic, on the instructions of the -- on -- sends instructions on the compilation of data for a report and as per the government's request, he asks for specific information on the theft of vehicles from TAS an oil from Ilidza, but in addition he requests that information be provided on serious crimes committed against Serbs in territories controlled by the "MUP of the former SRBiH." So, again, there's emphasise on crimes committed against the Serbs in documents that are coming from the MUP.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, we can see here, I've shown you a couple of examples, I can take you to one more example, and that is Exhibit P02759 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Witness asked what the question was. Could you tell the witness what the question was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. My question is we can see here that the RS MUP are concentrating on wanting information to be provided about serious crimes committed against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I would kindly ask that the witness be shown that as well. It is not on the page we are looking at.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to the following page. And, again, the following page in English. And it's under the note at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you see that there, Mr. Planojevic?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So we can see that there is an emphasis on crimes committed against the Serbs. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But if I may provide an explanation of the reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Up until that period, we had been receiving numerous reports from the ground regarding crimes committed against Serbs, particularly in Podrinje. And since we did not have any communications at all, certain inspectors would come to Pale personally in order to seek suggestions and guide-lines on how to act and whether they could receive any sort of assistance, given that they were understaffed in terms of professional personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, sorry --

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that that prompted this dispatch. And if I may add one thing. If you look at some documents that I drafted before this one, let's say, one from early June 1992, in that document, I issued an instruction to combat all forms of crime, including war crimes, crimes against civilians, POWs, et cetera, et cetera. So it appears that these two things are contradictory but if I may give you an additional explanation --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Mr. Planojevic, I want to focus on this. You mentioned your document that was dated in early June. This document here is dated the 26th of May, so this is before your document is issued. Now, wouldn't you -- the -- the head of the police should be requesting that information be provided about all serious crimes committed against all ethnicities, not just Serb -- persons of Serb ethnicities, shouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you are referring to me, this is how I acted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, if we can see Exhibit P02759 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Is it your case that this document is limiting the reports to Serb victims, cases where there are Serb victims?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So your base is this note? The last part, note.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It says it is also necessary to list the cases of serious crimes committed against the Serbs. But if we see the first page, it's not limiting to the Serb victims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The emphasise -- sorry, Your Honour. The case is -- our case is they're putting emphasis on crimes being committed against Serb victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could we have Exhibit 202759, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is this going to be tendered?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes. May I tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about the previous one, Djeric document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. I will be discussing the TAS cars later, but I seek to have that admitted as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I note that she didn't ask a single question about that document [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, she showed that and asked the [overlapping speakers] she showed that in lump sum and asked questions all together. I take it you have no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not really, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We admit them both.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter number 18388 will be Exhibit P6239 and 10834 will be Exhibit P6240.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now this is in response to Stanisic's 26 May 1992 order and this is from the CSB Banja Luka on the 12th of June. And the report includes information on crimes committed against the Serbian civilian population. So this is the information that's coming back to the ministry. Now, you mentioned your dispatch a moment ago of the 5 of June, and for the parties, that's Exhibit D01527. I don't intend to bring it up. You instructed the CSBs to pay attention to the discovering of the perpetrators of war crimes. And you -- you didn't limit it to -- to war crimes against Serbs, nor did it expressly include such crimes committed against non-Serbs either. But the SJBs were interpreting this instruction as including crimes committed against the non-Serbs [sic], and in 1992 in their daily reports they reported against -- on war crimes committed only against the Serbs. An example of that is Exhibit D01616. That's evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. In the transcript it says that I said "the SJBs were interpreting this instruction as including crimes against the non-Serbs." I in fact said, or, if I misspoke, I meant to say "including crimes against Serbs, and in 1992 in the daily reports they reported this." Mr. Planojevic, on 17th of June, 1992, the Presidency instructed the government to draft a decision on the establishment of a state documentation centre which will gather all genuine documents on crimes committed against the Serbian people during this war. Do you recall that instruction? And for the parties and the Chamber, that's Exhibit D00415. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall. I must explain to you that written communications were very often non-existent between me who was based in Vrace, and the remaining part of the ministry based in Pale. Cedo Kljajic and I, as operational heads of department, were based in one location, and due to that, it happens that some of the documents I have never seen before. Now, as for the fact that the minister gave me a free hand to deliver his dispatches as I felt suitable and to act accordingly, because I was the most highly trained professional in that respect, we started with four or five operatives initially without any communication devices, and you must bear that in mind --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, if I can interrupt you. We will get onto communications in a moment. But, for now I'm concentrating on what -- what information is coming out from the government. And you've just said that you don't remember seeing this 17 June 1992 instruction from the RS Presidency. Do you recall that in July 1992 the Presidency appointed members of the commission for investigating war crimes committed against the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina? And for the parties that's Exhibit D00444. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just before you answer, yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to avoid any confusion, it was said that that was a commission for the investigation of crimes or the documentation centre referred to earlier. Can we please make it clear what the question put to the witness pertained to?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, there's two different things. On the 17th of June the RS Presidency instructed the government to draft a decision on establishing a state documentation centre which will gather all genuine documents on crimes committed against the Serbian people. A month later, in July -- or in the month of July, the RS Presidency appointed members of the commission for investigating war crimes committed against the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you remember that commission being set up and members being appointed to it? It just requires a yes or a no answer.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I remember a commission where a certain lady named Gordana was appointed. Anyway, there was a commission, but I don't know what was its proper name. I think it was called the commission for investigating war crimes. One of the member's last names was Govedarica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In its report for April to December period the RS MUP reported: "The focus of the operative work in CSBs and SJBs was on detection, documenting and reporting members of the enemy army who had committed acts of genocide against the Serbian people, torched or destroyed immovable property, cultural and religious monuments and other assets." And that's Exhibit P02761. Again, Mr. Planojevic, we can see there is an emphasis on crimes being committed against the Serbian people. That was the focus of the operative work in the CSBs and SJBs according to the report, the MUP report, for the period April to December 1992.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible for me to see these documents on the monitor?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I won't be a moment. Your Honour, I'll come back to that. I'll re-call this document up and I'll come back to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, I want to ask you a few questions now in relation to the Republika Srpska being interested in investigating the car thefts and that's the Golfs from TAS. Prompted by the government - we saw the 24th of May, 1992, order earlier - Stanisic expended considerable resources to solve the problems of vehicle thefts, didn't he? You said that the theft of cars from the TAS factory was being tackled very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Ms. Sutherland. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland has been having a habit of putting a question to the witness and then not giving him any chance to answer it. So she just asked a question, can she please wait, let him answer. Or if she wasn't serious about asking a question, don't ask the question, ask some other question. But you can't put questions and not give the witness a chance to answer them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was simply taking the witness to something that he said which was exactly on the point of the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it -- it -- it's easier not only for the witness but also for the Chamber if you break down the -- your questions. Please proceed Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So, Mr. Planojevic, you said that the theft of cars from the TAS factory was being tackled very seriously, didn't you? You said that in the Stanisic trial. And that's at transcript page 16432.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In fact, one of your closest associates in the crime prevention department testified that operation TAS continued for a number of years and implemented investigative measures in the entire territory of the Republika Srpska as well as Serbia and Montenegro and could not name any comparable investigations in its -- in the magnitude that -- of -- of the efforts that were expended into solving this -- this vehicle problem. And that was Mr. Macar at transcript page 22929 to 22930. You would agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: What trial was that given in?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Stanisic/Zupljanin trial.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you like me to provide a comment and an explanation regarding this matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you agree with what I just said, that -- would you -- would you agree with what Mr. Macar said?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite sure what you said. I wasn't able to follow you. You wanted to say that the issue of the Golfs was not seriously investigated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No. That it was very seriously investigated. In fact, such considerable resources were put into it that -- that there was no other comparable investigations of that magnitude. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I have to explain to you that I obtained a diskette with chassis and engine numbers because quite a few -- a large number of those cars were already in Belgrade. Whenever such a vehicle arrived at the border crossing they were confiscated. After I had obtained this diskette I went to have a meeting with the most responsible vice-president of the executive committee and the president of the assembly and the army commander. The chief had already been shot dead by a local criminal which means that the local police station was virtually non-operational. A major by the name of Skipina appeared because we had the commander in that meeting, and he reported the fact that the crime called Pina [phoen] had taken some 20 golf vehicles from the TAS compound. So we were unable even to stop that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think your answer was unresponsive to my question. I put to you that the most considerable resources were put into this investigation and -- and according to Mr. Macar, there was no other comparable investigation of that magnitude. And I asked you whether you agreed with that. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to turn onto a different topic now, Mr. Planojevic. You said in your statement you've said earlier that there were no written -- there were no written documents at all, there was a communication breakdown, there was no way to know whether anyone received a dispatch that was sent, and, if so, who received it, and that you were not receiving reports either. The CSB were not acting in isolation. The -- Mico Stanisic directed the CSBs to send daily reports - and that's Exhibit P02758 - and the CSBs were regularly submitting such reports. You know, don't you, that the RS MUP daily bulletins derived from information that are submitted by the CSBs and the SJBs?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We have an exhibit in this case, Exhibit P02760, which is the MUP performance report for the period April to June 1992, and in that report, it notes that nearly 60 issues of the bulletin of daily events were published as a source of information for senior officials, mostly ministers and the prime minister. So it can be gleaned from this report that the CSBs were reporting to the RS MUP and their information was being contained in the bulletins, no?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And also in relation to the communication breakdown that you refer to, one of the first measures as -- as minister, Stanisic addressed the task of developing the RS MUP communications system by asking an experienced professional Serb policeman, Dragan Kezunovic, to accept the position of communications chief in April 1992. Do you -- you're aware of that, aren't you, that he appointed Mr. Kezunovic to the position of communications chief?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Kezunovic, yes. He was appointed, and he was based in Vrace as well. Now I remember. He spent most of his time there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the Trial Chamber has heard evidence that in the beginning the RS MUP headquarters had multiple means to communicate with its subordinate organs, including telephones, facsimile machines, short-wave and ultra short-wave radios and teleprinters. And this is from Exhibit P02743, pages 20 and 26. This is from Mr. Kezunovic's evidence. And he also provided -- yes, from his statement. He also provided evidence that when no other means were available, messages were delivered by human couriers, and I think -- and that's at page 21, and I think that you referred to that earlier when you said that you sent something to the field, did you not?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Very often communications were down so when there was something urgent to dispatch, couriers would be employed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And contrary to your statement that there was no communications between the RS MUP and the CSBs and their subordinate SJBs, we have evidence in this case - and this is P02761 - this MUP report that we were going to look at a moment ago which says that the RS MUP headquarters sent out 2.969 open dispatches and 1.300 coded dispatches, and during the same period it received 2.802 open dispatches and 1.601 coded dispatches, and, in addition, 9.585 short-wave radio connections were established during this period. So this information is -- is -- is contrary to what you say in your statement that there was no communications and no documents, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: This is not contradictory to my own statement. There was communication between areas where there was no combat, where there was peace. However, where we needed the communications to function the most, it didn't. As far as radio connections were concerned, that could not be treated as a functional communications system. I believe you understand what I'm saying. When I say "functional," I mean functioning for the purpose of the police work.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just while we have this document on the screen, if I can take you back to the page that I said that I would before. It's on e-court page 21 in the B/C/S in the middle of the page. And this was in relation to the focus of the operative work in CSBs and SJBs was on detection, documenting and reporting members of the enemy army who had committed acts of genocide against the Serbian people, et cetera. Do you see that there in the middle of the page?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: The third paragraph; right? Yes, I can see that now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. So returning to the issue of communications and reports, you said that you didn't receive any reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter number 24862, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I think you, in fact, say in your statement at paragraph 20 -- you say in your statement that you weren't receiving reports. This is a report from Mr. Milomir Orasanin and Dragisa Borovcanin dated the 30th of May, 1992, reporting on their work of Vogosca and Ilijas SJBs. Do you not recall receiving this report?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that I sent Orasanin there in order to inspect the situation after I'd been there at the beginning of June. I would have to read the report in order to jog my memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. In paragraph 20 you say, "We tried to sent inspections [sic] to certain places." You actually mention Milomir Orasanin in that paragraph. You say: "But as often as not, the people we sent to do this took advantage of the opportunity and simply travelled on and left the country." So we see here a report dated the 30th of May on their visit to the Vogosca and Ilijas SJBs. Now do you remember receiving this report?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I believe so. I said that I had sent Orasanin to that area. I would have to read the report to see what's in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you see there that they're reviewing the work?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm reading, if I may. I started a story about Vogosca, and I told you that it didn't function because of the attempted murder of the chief of the police there. There was no crime investigation police at the time --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, if I can interrupt you. I -- I don't want do get into the detail. My question was simply you say in your statement that you did not receive reports. I'm showing you a report that's dated the 30th of May when you were assistant minister, and I'm saying: Do you now recall receiving this report? And, if not, we can move on to another one.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I said that I had probably received it because I sent a man into the area. I didn't say that I had not received this report. I just wanted to read it, to remind myself of its contents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6241, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have on the screen Exhibit D01436, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Again, this is a report dated the 17th of June, 1992, on inspection conducted and the situation found at SJB Brcko, SJB Zvornik and partially the situation at SJB Bijeljina. And it refers to work conducted between the 29th of May and the 12th of June, 1992, by -- by two employees of the RS MUP, Dragomir Andan and Danilo Vukovic. So do you recall receiving this report?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that I'm reading this for the first time. I don't think I received this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were in the department on the 17th of June?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was working at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to turn now to a -- to another topic. You testified that you knew a person now deceased called Dusko Malovic who was the commander of a unit of some 20 to 30 men. You testified in the Stanisic/Zupljanin trial about that at transcript page 16445. Do you recall that? You were shown a list of --

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- special police platoon employees who performed their duties during October 1992 and were paid their salary for the month in advance. And that's 65 ter number 24849.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could call that onto the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now you testified in the Stanisic Zupljanin trial at transcript page 16455 that you knew six persons in addition to Malovic as being part of the special police platoon. And that was number -- no, besides number 1, Dusko Malovic; number 2, Boban Kezunovic; number 5, Nenad Stuparusic; number 10, Rajko Paunic; number 11, Danko Arbinja; number 12, Milenko Acimovic; number 14, Zoran Jolovic. And you also said that you knew number 27, Predrag Bartula, that he was a man who trained kick-box but you never saw him as part of your unit. Now, when you were interviewed in 2004, you said that this unit provided protection to the minister, Mico Stanisic, and then during proofing just before you testified, you said that except for a couple of minor errors the rest of the transcript was accurate. You then met with the Stanisic Defence team without an OTP representative being present and then you recanted about what said about the unit in terms of security and protection for the minister. You said that it was incorrect and that this unit only provided security for Stanisic on one occasion in July on a trip to and from Belgrade. Do you recall that, what I've just put to you?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I did not hear the last part of the your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, actually, just reviewing the transcript, first of all, I read out to you the names of the people that you recalled as being part of the special police platoon, and I read out those six names. You remember saying that in the Stanisic Zupljanin trial, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I said that I knew those people but not from the unit. I knew that they were unit members, and I said about that man, Bartula, that I was never close to them. So this is true. I knew most of those men by their nicknames.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that they were part of the special police platoon. And this is transcript page 16455.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: If that's what I said, then that's what I said. And then what?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then I just put to you that you were interviewed -- when you were interviewed you said that this unit had provided protection. However, you actually went back on that issue after you had -- after -- when you were interviewed in 2004 and you went back on that issue in 2010 just before you testified. Now that's right, isn't it, what I just put to you, those facts?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Partly. During my proofing session before I had any contacts with the Defence, I explained to the Prosecutor that when I said that he was protected, I meant that he was protected from attacks by enemy formations. He was escorted the way VIPs are normally escorted as he was travelling from Caparde to Karakaj. There was a collegium meeting in Belgrade and he was escorted to that meeting. There was a part where people always got killed. That's where he was escorted by five cars belonging to that unit. That was what I meant when I said that he was being protected. Furthermore, I had a total of three or four different contacts with Mico Stanisic during that period. I even explained for each of our contacts who provided escort and who protected him. And thirdly, Malovic's unit held the combat line throughout the entire month of May behind the school in Vrace. And then they were engaged in combat, as far as I can remember, in the territory of Dobrinja. Sometime towards the end of June, they lost two men there. One of them was nicknamed Glavonja, as far as I can remember. In other words, that was in May and June. I am convinced that that unit did not have any other activities but that engagement. When they escorted the minister during combat, the entire unit was involved in that. I apologise for this lengthy answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can have 65 ter number 24852, please. Now, Mr. Planojevic, we can see here this is the proofing note and I'm -- unfortunately, we don't have it in your language. But paragraph 1 says that you were met on the 19th of October and you confirmed that your transcript of the -- of the interview in 2004 was correct apart from a few minor errors, and it mentions the three minor errors that you picked up. And then it talks about Mr. Malovic only providing security on this one trip. Now, the information that you provided when you were interviewed in 2004 was something that you gave voluntarily about Mr. Malovic's unit. It wasn't something that was put to you as a question and then you were answering it. You actually volunteered it. And you proffered it, information in relation to a man called Ivan Curak being beaten by Malovic. And this is at -- in your OTP interview at page 65 of the English and page 67 of the B/C/S. And that is 65 ter number 1D21002. You talk about that. And then a little while later when you were discussing the attendees of the 11th of February meeting that you attended in Banja Luka, you were asked whether any of the attendees had any personal escorts. And you said that Malovic and his group of 20 to 25 men were all from the -- Sokolac and that Zoran Cvijetic as head of the CSB Sarajevo brought them and that Mico Stanisic took them from Zoran. Do you recall saying that when you were interviewed in 2004?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember what I said. First of all, I did not think it was important who escorted whom. Second of all, when Ivan was beaten, that happened in Vrace. And the minister was not there at all. I believe that it was in late May.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, no. It was in relation to talking about this gentleman that you then referred to Malovic for the very, very first time. And you talked about his unit. And then a little while later in the interview, you actually discussed that it was actually him and a group of 20 to 25 men that then came, and that Mico Stanisic took them from Zoran Cvijetic who had actually brought them. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember any details. I may have said that. However, whenever he crossed risk areas there was a combat unit that escorted him. I don't see any problem in that. However, when I spoke to the Prosecutor before my last trial, I explained him, and I can't remember his name, before the Defence even got involved. When they started eliciting details about the unit, then I provided a very detailed explanation. I adhere by all of those words because I spoke of what I had seen. I saw him three or four times. The fourth time I saw him from the hotel. And -- and on one occasion, he was escorted through Caparde. He had come to Vrace. Jasarevic was -- escort him in May 1992. Our second contact was in --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to -- I'm not talking about the times that you saw different people with Mr. Stanisic. I want to concentrate on what you said about Mr. Malovic. And after you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, I'm not sure how relevant, important this line of question is. But if you like to put such question I would like to put one by one. Why don't you show the witness what he said in interview and what -- it's a bit difficult for me as well to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. If we could go to page 80- -- 60 -- 65 in the English and page 67 in the B/C/S of Exhibit 1D21002.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we do that, while we're still here with this document, this is 24852.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The proofing note. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. What Ms. Sutherland put to this witness is contradicted by this note, and I think she has been unfair to the witness. If you look at the second paragraph of this note, you'll see that that was when he revealed to them about Malovic. And then if you look at the fourth paragraph of the note, it says that later --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Is it fair to do this exercise in the presence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I can could it outside of his presence but I think it's been unfair to the witness so far, and I'm trying to correct it. I think it is beneficial to the witness to hear that. But if you think that it would influence his answer, I can do it outside his presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since Ms. Sutherland is going to put her question again, let us see. And, if necessary, you can intervene again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Since we -- since this document is only in English maybe I could just point out to you to take a look at.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [Overlapping speakers] ... and I do apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, how much more would you need to conclude your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think I have about 15 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I take it that you need some time for your re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I suppose. But not too long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a break now so that you can some organise --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- the remainder --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- of your cross. Ver well. We will take a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, I must apologise to the Court and to Mr. Planojevic for misrepresenting the series of events in relation to the proofing that occurred when you were here last time. I don't know how I got it so mixed up in my head. I know I have been working on other -- other matters, but that doesn't explain it, so I hope my apology is accepted, and Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Very quickly, Mr. Planojevic, because there's a couple of other issues that I want to discuss with you. But I would just take you to the page in the interview in 2004 where you were talking about Mr. Malovic and his group.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 89 to 90 of the English and page 92 to 93 of the B/C/S. And that's 1D21002, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Planojevic, here you say in the beginning that was like a combat unit that came with Zoran Cvijetic to Sarajevo. For the first months they were protecting the line and you mentioned they were behind the school earlier. And it says here and they were participating in combat activities. After that, a certain number of men from that unit were taken by Mico and I don't know the exact number but there were usually around ten of them. And then you go on in the next answer. So there -- sorry. In relation to that answer you gave, you said that there were usually around ten of them which must mean that you had seen them on more than one occasion. You said a moment ago, just before the break, that they were only security for Mico Stanisic on this one occasion when you were travelling to Belgrade for the collegium in July 1992. But clearly doesn't this mean that -- that you saw them with him more than that one occasion in July?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was once in Kosuta where all of the units were billeted so that there was no need to provide security. When I provided a statement as a suspect in 2004, at the time, I didn't even think about or didn't think it was important and it was out of some kind of protest because I did not see them afterwards in combat. But, as I said, I only saw them when they escorted the minister. That is why I then said that they were providing security for him. I understood that it happened only when he was travelling. That's all the explanation I have. All I said is precisely the way it was. How did this come about? Well, of course, this is not made up, the story I provided in 2004. I can only explain by saying that I did not realise the importance of Malovic. That was the only reason. I have no other explanation. There's another thing which I all ready mentioned and that is that it is all true. I can't -- I can't recall every single time I ran into them so I can't even assert that they constantly provided his escort.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And it was Mico Stanisic that had the authority to -- to decide when and how these special units would be used; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I wouldn't call them, at least in my view, they were not a special unit. There was one special unit commanded by Karisik and Repija was his deputy. As for the rest, they could call themselves whatever they wanted but there were groups assembled by someone who took part in combat and believed to be special. So there was only Karisik's unit and Repija as his deputy, and later on it was Saric. That was the only special unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay, I want to move on. In paragraphs 26 and 27 of your statement you mention Batko. That's Veselin Vlahovac; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Vlahovic, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you said that you informed Mico Stanisic about him and also Djeric, the crimes that had been committed by -- by him. You said that after Djeric made a phone call, and you're not sure who to, that at -- that at first Batko disappeared from Grbavica for about ten days and on his return the army arrested him and detained him. However, that wasn't the end of the matter, was it? Because you know that after he spent some time in army detention he returned back to the area?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I have to go back a bit. I only heard about his crimes, as I explained in my previous statement and that was in Belgrade. Since there were no bodies, there was no crime until you discovered the bodies. That is why I, at the beginning, only started inquiring whether it was true because that was the story that went around Belgrade and to see whether it was indeed happening. It all was based on the assessment of two or three operatives, colleagues, who worked on it. They told me that there were some stories, and given the fact that he was the kind of person, I've already explained what kind of person he was and who he associated with, well, of course, then I first went to the minister and he said, given that he was indeed in paramilitary formations and one needed an armed force to arrest him, I think they wanted to use someone from the army, and two or three days later I sat down with the prime minister. I found it necessary to make the whole thing more serious and to engage in operative work to see whether it's true. Someone must have provided a signal, so he just went off -- under the radar. However, after that period, some ten days later he was arrested. I know that. And I even remember that we had agreed that the prime minister would call president directly. I don't know whether he managed to contact him, because he was unable when I was there, in order to have the man arrested. I don't know how long he was away for some ten or 15 days, but once he resurfaced he was retained by the army. I was then busy going about my private things, but, at the end, he was released. He was arrested, that's definitely so, and it was done by the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And do you know if he was ever tried during the war for the crimes he committed?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I read in a newspaper that even in Novi Sad there was an attempted murder that he was responsible for also during the war, in 1993 perhaps. And then again I read that in Podgorica there was an attempted murder as well, and then all trace of him is lost.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You know that he is being tried now by the BH State Court for crimes that he committed in May to September 1992. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I do know that, I read it in the papers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that the Yellow Wasps in paragraph 30 of your statement -- you only heard rumours that they killed some civilians in Celopek. The -- the -- the RS MUP took no measures against the Yellow Wasps and -- or -- or they didn't take measures until the Yellow Wasps began confiscating the Golf vehicles at a check-point in Karakaj; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to answer that question. I was unaware of their existence until they controlled me. I even accepted it in goodwill. And when I heard who I was [as interpreted], they said that they had data on what had gone to Belgrade, and I explained that I would send an inspector the next day, thinking they were acting in goodwill. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Planojevic, that's in your statement. My question was, as far as you're aware, the RS MUP took no measures against the Yellow Wasps until the point where they started confiscating Golf vehicles and also, if I may add to that, that Stanisic was harassed at a check-point by the Yellow Wasps, and within days, an operation was ordered led -- led by Mico Davidovic to have the paramilitary group arrested; that is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's not right. I have to correct you. That operation was being set up by the state -- well, that was right after my return, perhaps around the 15th of July. There were many problems, not only confiscating cars, there were all sorts of other things which I learned later, and the operation had to be set up operatively. First, it had to be investigated, who they were and how many, so it was first the state service who prepared the data. Perhaps only a month later they were arrested, all of them, during the night. I learned about it later. They were interviewed, and I don't know what was done later on whether they were prosecuted. I know they were all arrested and that the exercise of conducting interviews with them lasted for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But they weren't -- they weren't charged with crimes committed against non-Serbs, they were actually charged with theft of vehicles and so forth, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I really can't say about that because I was no longer in my position once it was implemented.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to show you a document now.

utterances.speaker: MS.  SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I can have 65 ter 24863, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a 1995 document, Mr. Planojevic. It's a report to the RS MUP from the State Security Department in relation to VRS members who captured 12 French soldiers. And it's a report dated the 27th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm told that it was not released, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Oh. Ms. Stewart is doing it as we speak, Your Honour. Unfortunately, Your Honour, we don't have a translation. I'll come back to the document. I won't waste time. While we're getting it released, I will turn to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just quickly, Mr. Planojevic, you were shown a document during your Stanisic Zupljanin testimony, and it's Exhibit P02978 [Realtime transcript read in error "P2078"] in our case and it doesn't need to be brought up on the screen, but it's a list of commendations for a number of persons, including members and units of the RS MUP who were receiving a medal for the -- for different things. And your name appears at number 139. And you testified in Stanisic/Zupljanin that you wrote to President Karadzic and told him you didn't want a medal but that you don't have a copy of this letter that you sent to Mr. Karadzic, but did you explain why you didn't want this medal in -- in -- in the letter? And this was a medal for the services to the nation.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: There was no explanation. As far as I recall, I even mentioned that there -- that was no time for explanations and that I didn't want to explain why I didn't want to receive it. What I said at the time was that I believed, because of the entire war situation where people were loosing lives and human life was at its cheapest, that no one deserved commendation. That was my position then. I'd rather not go into any specific reasons. I believe that's how I put it at the time. There will always be sufficient time to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The exhibit number you gave seems to be the different one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise. I will find the correct exhibit number and advise. We have document number 24863 released now. And, Your Honour, I just note that in e-court that document does come up when you put in P02978 which is the number that I gave. But in the transcript it reads "P2078" instead of "2978." I apologise if I misstated the number. I don't want that document on the screen. I would like to have 65 ter number 24863, 65 ter number, on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is the 1995 document from May, 27th of May, Mr. Planojevic. And it says here that the French soldiers on the Vrbanja bridge have been taken to the offices of Investbanka as hostages; is that right? That's the term that's used in the documents, "hostages"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or shall we ask the witness to read aloud?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, we can do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, can you just read the last -- last paragraph? The second-to-last paragraph. Sorry. Yeah, sorry, the first -- starting -- starting with the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well: "According to the latest operational information that we have at our disposal, members of our forces hold 12 French soldiers as hostages on the premises of the Investbank (the building closest to the Vrbanja bridge). They had captured them and taken them from the French check-point at the Vrbanja bridge. At the check-point, there are currently four to five of our soldiers holding two French soldiers hostage. However, they have been blocked by both French and Muslim forces."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Planojevic. That's --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And an English translation is being uploaded into e-court, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No question about this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, I can see this is signed "za." Do you know who signed this on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: It is possible that it was Tomo Puhalac. I'm not sure this is his handwriting. He was my deputy at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I seek to tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6242, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And thank you, Mr. Planojevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask you, Mr. Planojevic, to assist us in clarifying certain elements which surfaced during cross-examination. Did you know what -- who provided my security detail on a standing basis?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I didn't. I knew who your driver was, and, later on, I knew another two people, but it probably changed. We saw each other infrequently, and I suppose there were changes in their composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But they were employed by the MUP; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honour, I don't know that this arises --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I don't know that this arises from cross-examination. I didn't ask any questions about Mr. Karadzic's security.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can explain. I have to lay a basis so as to reach a full description, full image. I'll get to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't know how. Mr. Robinson, could you assist us a bit further.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think what Dr. Karadzic is getting at is the issue of Mr. Malovic and his escorting of officials which was raised in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber, as a member of the state security, what was the procedure when I travelled, myself or any other senior official that had to be escorted as per law?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: It had to be operationally covered. In other words, it had to be assessed whether there was any threat. Information had to be gathered on the level of threat and the particular points which were deemed dangerous. If necessary, it also included certain combat assets, especially in the area via Caparde which is something I mentioned. In keeping with such an assessment, the number of security detail is decided upon; that is to say, the strength of forces securing the passage. In order to answer your first question, at first I wasn't familiar with it because it was always up to the state security to deal with the security detail. I knew your driver. By September/October 1992, I moved to the state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As regards the permanent members of security detail, the combat security provided along the route, is it always the same?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: It is impossible to always have the same people. It depended on the area. If it was the area of Podrinje -- well, escort means providing a certain type of securing persons in movement. It always required local forces because there weren't enough men to cover it all, at all times. Frequently it meant a certain number of people, but they changed depending on their current engagement though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know who was on the permanent security detail of Minister Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was Jasarevic and Abazovic in most occasions, actually, on two or three or four occasions that we met. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Kezunovic was mentioned, and in his testimony he stated how many daily telegrams were required typically for the service to operate normally, provided communications were operational. Did you say today that you never received any reports or that you didn't receive a single -- a sufficient number of reports?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was isolated in Vrace. I must tell you that all the lines from our base went via Sarajevo. So at any moment, it was possible for those people in Sarajevo to cut us off. These lines went on from Sarajevo across the territory of the Federation so every post office was able to sever the communication lines. The only post office in the hands of the Serbian forces was the one in Ilidza. All the rest were in the Federation so that mail barely reached it. Since the analysis department was in Pale, and I can see that the analysts received some reports and that these communications worked a little bit better. But, anyway, I don't think that anything was working around Sarajevo and it was physically impossible for any mail to reach its destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where was the work station of Mr. Orasanin, the one you sent to Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: He was an inspector in the administration department. He didn't have a proper appointment letter, but he was working with the administration of the criminal investigation police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where was his workplace?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Mainly in Vrace, unless he was asked to help someone on the ground in Podrinje, Ilidza, and other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how did he send this -- report to you on the inspection that he had carried out in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was brought to me in -- personally. He -- he gave it to me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly? He makes a report and then comes in person to deliver it to you.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in which areas were you able to conduct investigations, criminal investigations.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we were restricted both in terms of communications and security. All the municipalities around Sarajevo held by the Serbian forces were something that was difficult to pass through. I sometimes didn't know who to send. And it was impossible to conduct any serious investigations from the point of view of a criminal investigation and tactical and other intelligence operations that we were absolutely unable to perform. If you want me to explain, I can give you at least ten reasons why that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am particularly interested in the note in P6240 on page 2, and I'm going to read it. It is necessary, if you know, to cite the cases of serious criminal offences against Serbs committed in the areas controlled by the MUP of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can you tell us, were you able to conduct investigations in the areas controlled by their MUP?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: All we could do was to collect intelligence only after the fact, but it was absolutely impossible to carry out an investigation work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did you gather intelligence about the events taking place in the territory beyond our control and where you had no access, in order to investigate?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Mainly through exchanges of individuals or from individuals who managed, one way or another, to escape from the territory under the Muslim control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who took statements from these individuals and what was done with those statements?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: It depended. Sometimes it was done by the officials from the National Security Service, and if there was insufficient personnel, people from the criminal investigation department would become involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I don't know how this arises from cross-examination, this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not related to the emphasis of the investigation? Let us see how it evolves. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, can you tell us whether Gordana, I think her last name, Bundalo, and Mr. Govedarica, what was their occupation and where were they employed?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that Govedarica was a photographer in the press centre. I think I'm not wrong. I think he was a photographer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was either of them employed in the MUP and were they criminal investigation experts?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. It has nothing to do with the Ministry of the Interior. I understand that to be a state commission, if I understood the question correctly, the commission that was set up to establish crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Miroslav Toholj.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Toholj. I see that the LiveNote is blocked. Was he the director of this other state centre for documentation and records of crimes against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was Mr. Toholj's profession?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: He was an author, a journalist, if I'm not mistaken, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us now what is the difference between investigation and documenting in the territories where we were unable to conduct investigations?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: The process of documenting events boiled down to, I think, photographing the events or recording them in some other way, as well as by taking witness -- statements from eye-witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How is that different from an investigation carried out in the territories that were accessible to us?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I said that a whole series of intelligence and operative and technical measures have to be undertaken, starting with establishing trace evidence, conducting interviews, carrying out an on-site investigation, a forensic investigation, and carrying out certain analyses, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, concerning the area where we had access more or less, that is to say, in the areas under the Serb control, was it possible for us to carry out special investigations of crimes against Serbs? So what was the attitude towards the perpetrators and the victims in the legal sense and the criminal sense that was taken by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat? I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: Did it make sense for us to collect information about the crimes -- committed by Muslims against Muslims in their territory?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what was the attitude of the investigating organs and the police and the MUP towards the crimes committed in the territory accessible to us. More or less, what was their attitude towards the ethnic background of the perpetrators and the victims? Was any distinction made in that sense?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, and I don't want to talk about the areas that I have no information about, we did not make any difference. Whenever I received intelligence about a certain area, and that pertained to this period of two or three months around Sarajevo, we treated both the victims and the perpetrators in the same manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
